Cormac O’KeeffeResearch and Innovation Director, Bibliothèques Sans Frontières

Three ways we work on AI

Offline AI

AI tools that work for everyone, even with no internet connection.

National-language data

Community-created datasets for under-resourced languages (the AI Social Club).

AI literacy

Equipping citizens with the skills to navigate a world with AI.

Lands on the thesis. Transition to the evidence.

The gap shows up in the benchmarks

The same model, scored on the same test, across languages:

Linguistic-knowledge benchmark leaderboard data. Best model shown (Gemini-3.1 Pro).

Top models score ~91% in English, ~87% Hausa, ~86% Kiswahili, but fall to ~77% Yoruba and ~69% Nyankore, and drop further for smaller models. Capability is real but uneven. This sets up the two Senegal polls.
One minute. Most people guess far too optimistic.
Click to reveal. ~8.6% only recently, only with a Wolof-specific model; off-the-shelf is 40–97%. Source: Senegal NLP survey, arXiv 2601.09716.
One minute.
Click to reveal. Essentially one system, 2026. This is exactly what the national-language work targets.

One country, eight national languages

Senegal recognises eight national languages (Wolof, Pulaar, Sérère, Soninké, Mandinka, Joola, and more recently Balant and Saafi-Saafi). Lowest published speech word-error rate per language. Source: Senegal NLP survey, arXiv 2601.09716.

Wolof ~8.6%, Sérère ~20%, Pulaar ~24%; the rest, including Balant and Saafi-Saafi, have no measured performance at all. The gap isn’t only in the scores, it’s in which languages anyone bothered to measure.

How do you do AI without the cloud?

Transition to the offline approach.

Why offline, not cloud

Generative AI assumes constant, cheap, high-bandwidth connectivity, the opposite of daily reality in rural Senegal, DRC, Nigeria and Ukraine.

  • Connectivity is limited, expensive or absent
  • Devices run on low power, off-grid
  • Sensitive data must never leave the device

BSF’s five principles

  • Equity and inclusion
  • Frugality and offline-first design
  • Open source and digital commons
  • Community governance and participation
  • Public-interest AI infrastructure
Offline-first is a requirement, not a preference.

One playbook

Small models

Quantised models running on Android, a Raspberry Pi or a Kajou microSD, with no cloud call at inference.

Retrieval + pre-generated content

A large model builds a vetted knowledge base once, upstream. Users then search it offline, and every answer points to its source, with no live generative AI at the moment of use. Retrieval and pre-generation are deployed together, as one solution.

Is this still “AI”? And why build it this way?

Let the provocation sit, then put the poll up. It matters for regulation, evaluation, and what users think they’re trusting.
One minute. People tend to pick one reason; the point is that all of them hold at once.
Click to reveal: all of the above. No live hallucination, runs on modest hardware, no data needed at use, near-zero cost per query. Retrieval and pre-generation are one solution.

Three architectures, three trade-offs

Model on the device

Redline. A ~321M-parameter model generates answers locally. Nothing leaves the device.

Content made off-device

Teacher Assistant. A large model builds the library once; the device only searches it.

Hybrid

kSanté, Karibu Prof. Core use is offline, but an online model handles the ~10% of questions the offline base can’t answer.

“Fully offline” is rarely absolute: be precise about where the model actually runs.

This is the honest version of the on-device-vs-not question. kSanté calls an online model when offline search fails, so it’s hybrid, not pure pre-generated.

Teacher Assistant

Problem. Around half of primary teachers in Senegal lack basic certification; rural teachers are professionally isolated.

Solution. An offline assistant retrieving curriculum-aligned lesson plans from plain-language queries. 5,882 lesson plans across 10 subjects and 6 grade levels.

Results. 82% of retrieved results rated usable. Deployment planned on 70 Ideas Cubes and 700 phones in Kédougou.

Partners: Senegal Ministry of Education · Enabel · DG INTPA (EU)

Generation was a one-time cloud step. That speed is the point, and the risk; we come back to it with the bias audit.

kSanté

Problem. Senegal has about 20 doctors per 100,000 people. Community health workers are often the only point of care, working from French protocols in non-French-speaking communities.

Solution. An offline Q&A assistant over 15,000 vetted question-answer pairs from official health documents, French and Wolof, adapted to local realities, plus a 14-module e-learning course.

Pilot (Saint-Louis, 2,000 health workers). 92% used the card; 91% used the AI assistant; 90% of ~2,000 real answers rated relevant; +12.2% knowledge gain; 83% say they treat patients better.

Partners: Senegal Ministry of Health · Gates Foundation · Institut Pasteur

Use the Saint-Louis pilot numbers throughout. Candid nuance for the Q&A: the assistant is used 52% at home, 24% at work, not yet mostly in the moment of care. An RCT with 600 workers reports in June.

Karibu Prof

Problem. Primary teaching in Senegal happens in French, a language some teachers don’t fully master.

Solution. Personalised reading and writing practice delivered offline via microSD, with an online AI writing tutor. Content covers classroom language, families, school administration, and subject vocabulary from the national curriculum.

Pilot. +23% in French proficiency (pre/post), effect size 0.96, NPS 64.

Partners: Ministry of Education · INEADE · FID / AFD · Eval-Lab

We look hard at that +23% in a moment.

Redline

Problem. People supporting survivors of conflict-related sexual violence in Nigeria, DRC and Ukraine need clear answers from dense legal texts, and their questions are too sensitive to leave the device.

Solution. A dual-mode assistant: a ~321M-parameter model fully offline on hardware as modest as a Raspberry Pi, and a larger online assistant for connected settings. Both cite the exact Guidebook passage.

Results. 96% user satisfaction (80% in Ukrainian).

Partners: CDCS · Fondation Mukwege · UN (OSRSG-CAAC)

The online assistant on the Mukwege Foundation’s Red Line site

Set up the dilemma. The poll is next.
Two minutes. Ask one or two to defend their vote aloud while results come in.
Click to reveal: both. Twist from L10: the Rwanda study found frontier models beat local clinicians and were far cheaper. So why go small? What did that study not measure? (Real-world outcomes, data flows, who controls the system.) Who decides this trade-off: funder, developer, or user?

Two more in the portfolio

Tutobac

A baccalauréat revision assistant that answers from the textbooks students are examined on. Pass rates in the region sit around 47%, and private tutoring is out of reach for most.

Tirailleurs sénégalais

In development with the Ministry of Education: a tool for sharing national memory, French first, national languages (Wolof, Pulaar, Sereer, Mandinka, Joola, Soninké) next.

Fast. Less evidence for each, so they share a slide.

We tested it with teachers

Action research on the Teacher Assistant.

A field test, not a demo

In January 2026 we sat with 16 primary teachers in Kédougou and Saraya, showed them the app and the AI-generated lesson plans, and asked them to validate the content.

We recorded what they understood, what they would ask the tool, and what they wanted changed.

Real action-research data (KoboToolbox, Jan 2026). Sets up the poll.

What teachers told us

  • The content matched the curriculum; they said they’d use the plans “very often”
  • Fixes were about form: present the plan as a three-column table
  • And about vocabulary: rename “introduction” to the official term (imprégnation / situation problème)
  • One recurring, non-content problem: the on-screen text was too small to use comfortably

The fix was interface and terminology, not a better model.

Echo of L10’s first paper: the model alone was accurate, but people using it did no better. The interaction is often the bottleneck.

Drawn verbatim from teachers’ responses (Q37–Q42).
Hier, Saliou, un élève de CE2 à Thiès, a gagné un concours de lecture. Il a lu un livre sur l’histoire du Sénégal. Sa récompense est un dictionnaire.Yesterday Saliou, a Year-3 pupil in Thiès, won a reading contest. He read a book on Senegal’s history. His prize is a dictionary.
Ta petite sœur Fatou veut aider votre maman à préparer un plat sénégalais. Elle ne sait pas faire le Yassa. Tu lui écris une note pour lui expliquer les grandes lignes.Your little sister Fatou wants to help your mum cook a Senegalese dish. She doesn’t know how to make Yassa. You write her a note explaining the main steps.

Two lesson contexts from the Teacher Assistant (French original, English below).

Two minutes in pairs, then answer on phones. Collect a few, then move to the audit.
Read some out. Then the next slide: what did we audit, and the MCQ.
One minute. Everyone has seen the pattern; the question is which is most frequent.
Click to reveal: girls + domestic roles, 2,200+ instances. The full table is in the note. Stress the method’s limit: automated co-occurrence counts flag patterns, not proven prevalence; each case needs human review.

What do you do about it?

  • Regenerate the content with better prompts and guardrails?
  • Filter the existing library?
  • Train teachers to spot and challenge stereotypes as they teach?
  • Adapt to local realities so content reflects the community, not a default?

BSF’s response included a workshop with teachers, “Casser les stéréotypes,” rather than treating it as a purely technical fix.

Where did the bias come from: the generating model, the curriculum sources, or both?

No single right answer; this is the discussion.

Present it straight, as you would to a funder. Then the funnel.

Designing the trial

The next phase is a randomised trial with Eval-Lab and the Ministry of Education: 250 teachers, a control group, in-person assessment before the SD cards go out, deploying mid-December.

But a sample isn’t neutral. The way you choose who’s in the trial shapes what the result can tell you.

Set up the poll: who gets measured is a design choice, not a given.
One minute.
Click to reveal: B. Then the other design choices (widened recruitment, 75/25 mix, TNEF screening). Each trades representativeness for feasibility; evaluation is a design problem, not just measurement.

What do our numbers actually measure?

90%
kSanté answers rated relevant, on ~2,000 real questions
+12.2%
kSanté knowledge gain, pre/post test
96%
Redline user satisfaction (80% Ukrainian)

What does each tell you, and what doesn’t it? A satisfaction score, a knowledge test, and a relevance rating measure three different things, and none is the same as better health outcomes.

Evaluation is political too: the evidence standard decides what gets scaled. Self-report isn’t outcome; relevance isn’t accuracy.

Risk and accountability

Transition into the governance questions.

Where would the law put these?

Unacceptable

Banned: social scoring, manipulation of vulnerable groups.

High risk

Education, health, essential services. Strict obligations.

Limited

Transparency: users must know they’re talking to AI.

Minimal

No specific obligations.

The EU AI Act sorts systems by risk. A reading tutor that just offers practice is limited risk. The same tool scoring pupils for grade placement is a different matter.

Two caveats worth holding: these high-risk obligations apply only from December 2027, and a Senegal-only deployment is outside the Act’s territorial scope.

Verify the Dec 2027 date against the primary text before presenting. Set up the poll next.
One minute.
Click to reveal: high risk (Annex III, education). Then the caveats: it applies from Dec 2027, and it doesn’t reach a Senegal-only deployment. For BSF the Act is a governance benchmark, not a legal duty.

Access scales in months. Accountability doesn’t.

Scaling AI to many more learners without scaling accountability can globalise harm as fast as benefit.

Who certifies that a tool is suitable for a given classroom, curriculum or language? Who owns failures involving children’s data? Who carries liability when a ministry, a school, an NGO and a vendor all share the workflow?

The frameworks to lean on

  • UNICEF, Guidance on AI and Children 3.0 (2025)
  • UNESCO, Guidance for Generative AI in Education (2023)

These give governments and NGOs concrete requirements, rather than leaving accountability to arrive years after access.

Use the accountability provocation to open discussion; anchor on UNICEF and UNESCO as the real frameworks.

Who is AI built for?

And who gets to decide: the funder, the developer, or the people who have to live with the answer?
